<!-- chapter: craft/episodic-shortform.md -->
# Episodic Short-Form: The AI Mini-Drama Pipeline

The most durable format in AI short-form video right now is not a single short, it is a *series*. Numbered episodes, one emotion each, voice-led, cliffhanger endings, and a caption that is itself the hook. This chapter adapts the genre into a repeatable production pipeline: nine stages, hard budgets, nine quality gates. The craft lesson underneath is old: a serial lives or dies on the bible, the arc, and the cut, AI only changes which of those costs the most money.

## The observed case

The pipeline below was reverse-engineered from the TikTok account **FutureGalaxyStories** (@uq6ctqxxc8), bio *"Creating stories with AI, capturing every moment through visuals"*, 358.8K followers, 6.3M total likes at the time of analysis (Oct 2026). The genre is the AI emotional mini-drama: tearjerker family stories told in numbered episodes, the same genre the `storyreel` skill in the guide's skill library was built from.

The representative episode: **"Episode 3, A 2-Year-Old Girl Took a Taxi Alone Just to Find Her Daddy"**, 82 seconds, 128K plays, 3,187 likes, 722 saves, 89 shares, 29 comments. The numbers worth studying are not the views; they are the *saves and shares relative to plays*, that ratio is the cliffhanger working. People don't save single jokes. They save things they intend to follow.

*(Episode-pipeline research, Oct 2026, observed case. Single-source, flag: the platform analytics came from the episode page itself, not an independent audit.)*

## The mini-drama boom, why the format is winning (Oct 2026)

Since this chapter was first written, the genre stopped being a niche observation and became the platform's headline story:

- **TikTok has been promoting episodic series since June 2026**, and mini dramas are now the fastest-growing *new* category on the platform (buytiktokaccount.com, single-source, flag).
- Typing "microdrama" into TikTok search now opens a dedicated **"TikTok Short Drama"** section: vertical 9:16 episodes, 1 to 3 minutes each. Series like *Reborn After He Chose Her*, *Spoiled by the CEO's Family*, and *My Fluffy Alpha Husband* have accumulated up to **455.7M views per series** (tiktoktiktoktiktok.substack.com, Oct 2026, single-source).
- Sensor Tower's *State of Short Drama Apps 2026*: short-drama apps passed **850M global downloads in Q1 2026 (+140% YoY)**, with average daily viewing at 25 minutes by April 2026 (+85% vs January 2025) (archyde.com, Sept 2026).
- DoubleVerify (Sept 2026): microdramas are **1 to 2 minute serialized episodes** built on romance, revenge, and frequent cliffhangers; Omdia puts global 2026 revenue at **$14B** (up from **$11B** in 2025, the US accounting for $1.5B, EIN Presswire, Oct 2026 release, single-source). DoubleVerify also flags brand-suitability risk (adult/violent content in some microdramas), the guide's revenge-arc lane stays non-graphic.
- In China, PhilSTAR Life (Oct 2026) reports **120,000+ microdramas released between January and March 2026, 95% of them AI-generated**, citing Chinese state media and CNN (flag the sourcing chain); Variety describes the AI short-drama shift as faster, more scalable, lower-threshold production. This is consistent with the earlier ~90% AI-generated figure (Kuhn), the Chinese market is now majority-synthetic.
- The platforms are building the rails, not just the audience: TikTok's **Drama Center**, introduced at its June 2026 Apps Summit, handles series management, multilingual translation, and revenue sharing for in-app Mini Dramas (Technode, June 2026); TikTok + creator agency Amplify launched **"The Next Episode"**, a program funding creator-led series instead of one-off posts (Metricool 2026 creator timeline; TikTok Newsroom).
- And governments are now co-funding the *craft*: on Oct 1, 2026, Singapore's IMDA and TikTok Singapore launched a **Microdrama Programme** training media professionals from 20 accredited companies to develop 50 to 100 episodes of 1 to 3 minutes over 6 to 9 months, with a dedicated **AI-enabled animation track** covering prompt engineering, character consistency planning, VFX quality review, and ByteDance's Seedance 2.5, plus paywall and monetization training (Xinhua / Television Asia Plus / Marketing-Interactive, Oct 2026). When a national programme teaches character consistency as curriculum, the locked-bible discipline in this chapter stops being genre advice and becomes the industry's training syllabus.
- The institutional read is widening. Sundance Collab and TikTok's **Micro-Series Challenge** (deadline Sept 9, 2026) asked applicants for a logline, character bios, a full series synopsis, *scripts for the first 30 episodes*, and a 1 to 3 page series bible, this chapter's G0 artifacts, as a submission form (reported via a creator post on LinkedIn, single-source, flag). Two caveats: the challenge barred generative AI from the *submissions* (development craft, not tool endorsement), and the deadline has passed. And TikTok itself is becoming a producer: Business Insider (March 24, 2026) reported TikTok casting actors for soap-opera-style micro-dramas and filing a US trademark for "TikTok Drama," with industry estimates putting the US mini-drama market at ~$1.4B (reported via newsmissinglinkhub.com, flag the chain). TikTok reported (June 2026) that short dramas recorded 2.26B global downloads in 2025, +140% YoY in Q1 2026 (alvinology.com).
- The AI-native platforms are building *worlds*, not just episodes. Shortical (Oct 2026) launched *Bound by Fire*, its first fully AI-generated original micro-drama, with the AI cast continuing "off-screen lives" on social media between episodes, behind-the-scenes videos and interviews generated by agentic AI (PR Newswire, company-claimed). The craft read: the cast living between episodes is a *distribution mechanic*, not a new format, it's the day-in-the-life format pointed at a drama's cast, keeping the audience inside the world between cliffhangers. File it as a technique to steal, not a lane to add.
- The counterweight to all of it: DataEye's H1 2026 report counts **221,900 new AI and animated dramas released on Douyin** in six months, and only **1,055 cleared 100M views (a 0.48% hit rate)**; The Paper's Sept 1 writeup puts break-even at ~50M views and finds **98.7% failed to break even** (reported via newfortunetimes.com and mitrade, flag the chain). Costs collapsed in the same window: CCTV reports the AI short-drama cost fell from ~5,000 yuan per minute early in the year to a few hundred (via enterprisewired). DataEye VP Lin Qiwen's read, paraphrased: AI isn't lowering costs so much as lowering the threshold for losing money. The oversupply argument for this chapter is blunt, when 220,000 shows compete for a finite audience, the ones with a bible, a locked voice track, and a cliffhanger are the 0.48%.

**Boom refresh (wave 38, Oct 2026), the funnel's price tag is now public.** A DramaBox-vs-ReelShort comparison (Oct 2026) puts the user-facing economics of the drama-app funnel in numbers: the first episodes are free, the rest coin-gated; finishing one series costs the viewer **$10 to 20**, heavy users up to **$80/month** (YouTube creator video, single-source). This is the demand side of the pipeline's G7 funnel CTA ("more inDrama↓"): the tease converts because the app stores have already trained the audience to pay per episode. On the supply side, carry both figures honestly: Appfigures' **$1.2B** = consumer spending (gross in-app), MPA's **$785M/$1.05B** = estimated revenue, different denominators, not competing facts (creator-economy research, Oct 2026). And a second monetization lane opened for serialized creators: Spotify's **Partner Program expands to 37+ markets starting Oct 20, 2026** (announced Sept 17; Spotify Newsroom + TechCrunch + RAIN News, via marketingnewsroom, corroborated, [verified]): the bar is 3 episodes + 2,000 consumption hours + 1,000 engaged audience in 30 days, payout is Premium video revenue share + 50% of ad revenue. It is audio-native with a video-payout tier, a lane for the voice-led, dialogue-heavy series this pipeline produces, not a replacement for the TikTok funnel.

This is validation, not a trend to chase, the pipeline in this chapter *is* the thing the platforms are now rewarding. Why the format wins, in platform-mechanics terms:

- **Serialization is the follow mechanic, and TikTok tests for it.** TikTok's distribution is interest-graph, not social-graph: every upload is tested against a small audience pool and widened only if early signals clear the gates (Hootsuite, Vamp, fivebbc, all three agree). An episode that ends on a cliffhanger with a numbered next part manufactures the follower the algorithm can't give you: someone who returns unprompted.
- **Watch time + completion rate are the dominant ranking signals.** The three sources agree on the order, watch time/completion first, then rewatches, shares, saves; one marketing study estimates the pair at 40 to 50% of ranking weight (DMA, single-source, treat as lore). One emotion per episode *is* a completion-rate design: nothing leaks the viewer's attention because there is only one thing to attend to. The genre's 60 to 150s band at high completion outcompetes shorter, leakier clips (DMA lore: a 60s video at 80% completion beats a 15s clip at 95%).
- **Cliffhangers are built for sends.** On Instagram Reels the #1 ranking signal is **sends per reach** (Mosseri, via virvid.ai / CreatorFlow), and a cliffhanger is the most sendable thing a video can be: *"you have to see what happens next."*
- **The Oct 1, 2026 Shorts originality update REWARDS this format.** YouTube now prioritizes original content in Shorts recommendations and reduces reach at the *channel level* for accounts that mainly aggregate or re-upload (announced by Creator Liaison Rene Ritchie via Creator Insider video + TeamYouTube post; Social Media Today, Oct 1, 2026). An original serialized series is the exact opposite of a clipping channel. The same gate exists on TikTok, which does not recommend reused or unoriginal content (viral.app, citing TikTok docs, Sept 2026). And TikTok's own AI-labeling rule costs nothing in reach: the Newsroom's Oct 1 update says over three billion videos have been labeled AI-generated since the program began, and TikTok's AI-content page states the AIGC setting does not affect distribution when the video complies with the Community Guidelines (reported via blog.evolvedlotus.com, Oct 8, 2026, single-source on the figures). Label AI episodes as AI; skipping the label is the risk, not the label itself. Policy-summary detail worth knowing (usefastlane.ai, storrito.com, secondary summaries, not the guidelines text): the labeling requirement targets *realistic-looking* people/scenes; generic text-to-speech narration and anime-style art are exempt, and TikTok auto-labels at scale via C2PA Content Credentials. Voice-led mini-dramas still turn the label on, the realistic-people trigger fires on the visuals. Everything in the nine stages below produces *original* footage, this pipeline was compliant before the rules changed.
- **YouTube's Feb 2027 monetization threshold is the other shoe.** Separately from the Oct 1 reach change, YouTube announced (Aug 2026, effective **Feb 1, 2027**) that Shorts Creator Pool earnings will require 10M qualified Shorts views on a rolling 90-day basis for *all* monetized creators, fall below and Shorts revenue pauses for the month (billo.app, citing YouTube's published Partner Program changes; gizbot.com). New Partner Program applicants need 1,000 subscribers plus 8,000 qualified watch hours in 365 days or 20M qualified Shorts views in 90 days. The three rules are separate (readus247.com, Oct 2026): (1) Shorts recommendation ranking, the Oct 1 change; (2) Partner Program reused-content policy, unchanged; (3) the Creator Pool revenue split, unchanged by Oct 1. A channel can keep its monetization and still lose its audience. Two useful details: YouTube gave no start date for the reach cut, and channels that switch to original work get their reach re-evaluated (Ritchie, reported via marketingnewsroom.com). The pipeline's position from day one: original footage, serialized, no aggregator behavior, nothing to retrofit.

The craft consequence: the deep moat (bible, arc, voice-first cut) is now also the platform moat. AI makes the footage cheap; the serialization makes it distributed.

## The genre anatomy, why the format works

Each of these is a design decision you can steal for any series, on any platform:

- **Numbered serialization is the follow mechanic.** "Episode 3" does more work than any hashtag: it tells a first-time viewer there is an Episode 4, which is the only promise that converts a viewer into a follower. Never post an episode without a number.
- **The caption IS the hook.** The observed formula: `[Episode N] + [one-line emotional stake] + [CTA]`. The caption names a character and a stake legible in one sentence, *"a 2-year-old girl took a taxi alone just to find her daddy"*, parenting, waiting, loss, reunion. These are stakes a stranger understands in two seconds. The first three seconds of picture restate the caption visually: a toddler alone in a taxi looking for her father. Caption and opening shot say the same thing; neither makes the viewer read twice.
- **60 to 150 seconds, one emotion per episode.** The runtime band is a craft constraint, not a platform setting: one episode carries exactly one emotion (grief, relief, dread, pick one word). Two emotions in 90 seconds reads as noise. The beats structure serves the single emotion: hook line in the first 3 seconds → 3 to 5 simple beats → a dedicated shot for the emotional turn → the cliffhanger.
- **Voice-led, not music-led.** Narration and dialogue carry the story; there is no reliance on trending audio. This is what makes the genre agent-producible: a locked dialogue track is deterministic, cheap, and version-controllable, where trending-audio strategy is not.
- **Cliffhanger endings, always.** Every episode ends mid-beat or on an unanswered question, never the resolution. The resolution is what Episode N+1 *is*. The craft name for this is the soap-opera pacing beat: gut-punch, then a question or an interrupted line.
- **The funnel CTA.** "More inDrama↓" teases a longer cut on a drama app. That is an external business funnel; the production pipeline produces the TikTok episode itself. Steal the shape (tease the next thing), not the destination.

The deep moat is not the animation, the genre's visuals are slow, simple, character-consistent frames; *the story does the work, not the animation.* The moat is the arc: a locked character bible, per-line voice-first editing, and dialogue-locked cuts. Everything else is execution.

## Four more working serialized formats (Oct 2026)

The mini-drama pipeline above is the flagship, but the boom is wider than one genre. Four more serialized short-form formats are demonstrably working right now. Each follows the same skeleton, numbered episodes, one unit of tension per episode, cliffhanger endings, with a different engine under it. Each entry: the format, why it works, and a fictional worked episode-block example showing the block structure.

### 1. POV micro-series, "you" are the protagonist

**The format.** Second-person scenarios, one per episode, numbered: *"Episode 1 … POV: You insulted a stranger yesterday… and today he's your billionaire boss"*, the "Hallway series" by @quiet.truths742 (76.4K likes, 134 comments on Episode 1; TikTok, Oct 2026). Each episode is a single encounter with one power reversal; the camera is the viewer's eyes.

**Why it works.** The "you" casts the viewer, no character introduction needed, no bible to lock, and the stakes are instant (status, embarrassment, desire). It inherits the mini-drama pacing (gut-punch → reversal → cliffhanger), but the cliffhanger is always social: *what happens when he sees you tomorrow?* The comment section does the distribution work, viewers tag the friend who "would absolutely do this," which is sends-per-reach fuel.

**Worked episode-block example** *(fictional, shows the block structure, not a real series):*

- Format: POV series · Episode 4 · Emotion: **dread**
- Stake: you borrowed your roommate's jacket, the stain won't come out
- Hook visual (first 3s): your hands frantically scrubbing fabric in a bathroom sink, coffee brown spreading
- Beats: (1) the spill, frozen mid-panic; (2) flashback: the roommate lending it this morning, *"take care of it"*; (3) the knock at the door, she's home early; (4) the turn: the designer label, it cost four figures
- Cliffhanger: the bathroom door handle turns, freeze on your face
- Keyframe scenes: sink scrub close-up / flashback handoff / designer label macro / door handle mid-turn

### 2. "Day in the life" AI character vignettes

**The format.** A recurring AI character, 15 to 60 second episodes from its daily routine, one small event per episode, no multi-episode plot required. An AI-anime creator guide (autoweeb.com, 2026) reports that **short serialized content with a recurring protagonist outperforms one-off images in both completion rate and subscriber conversion**, and that "day in the life" character vignettes work in the 15 to 60s range.

**Why it works.** The character IS the series, familiarity compounds. Plot overhead is near zero (routine + one surprise), so the nine-stage pipeline runs at its cheapest: the anchor paragraph and voice ID do the heavy lifting, and every episode is four keyframes from one world. The follow mechanic is parasocial, not narrative: viewers return to *see how she's doing*, the way they check a friend's story. The bible is the whole show here, G0 discipline is the quality bar.

**Worked episode-block example** *(fictional):*

- Format: day-in-the-life · Episode 12 · Emotion: **comfort**
- Stake: Rin the night-shift barista makes the 2 AM regular's drink before he orders
- Hook visual (first 3s): espresso machine steaming in a dark shop window, rain on glass
- Beats: (1) rain on the window, empty café; (2) the regular's shadow at the door; (3) the turn: Rin is already steaming the milk, she remembered
- Cliffhanger: he slides a folded note across the counter, freeze before it opens
- Keyframe scenes: rainy window / door shadow / steaming milk close-up / folded note mid-slide

### 3. Revenge / betrayal arcs, the justice ladder

**The format.** A multi-episode revenge plot where each episode delivers one injustice and one retaliatory move: betrayal → discovery → the plan → the takedown → the reveal. OutlierKit's 2026 niche data gives betrayal & revenge storytelling a **21x breakout rate** with $20 to $25 CPMs on YouTube (outlierkit.com, creator-reported ranges). In short drama, ReelShort's *Your love is my poison* (60-second episodes of betrayal, hidden identities, second-chance romance, viral early 2026) and Playlet's *Never Betray the Woman Who Built You* (affair reveal in minutes, revenge escalating episode by episode) show the funnel pattern: free episodes as TikTok/Reels clips, the full series behind the drama app, *"Continue the story here 👉🏻 Find the full series on the ReelShort app"* (md-eksperiment.org watch guides, 2026; TikTok promo posts).

**Why it works.** Catharsis is the most portable emotion on the internet: the viewer arrives already angry on the heroine's behalf, so the hook costs nothing. The justice ladder is a natural episode map, each episode is one rung, and the cliffhanger is always *the next move*. Finales get the thesis line (the pipeline's G7 rule), which is why these series convert to the paid funnel: the thesis is the product.

**Craft caution.** DoubleVerify flags that some microdramas carry adult, violent, or criminal content and advises brand-suitability review (Sept 2026). The guide's lane: non-graphic, feel-good vengeance, the betrayal is emotional, the revenge is a comeuppance, never gore. A revenge series with the pipeline's single-emotion discipline reads as empowerment; without it, it reads as slop.

**Worked episode-block example** *(fictional):*

- Format: revenge arc · Episode 6 · Emotion: **triumph**
- Stake: Nadia exposes the business partner who stole her designs, at his own launch event
- Hook visual (first 3s): a runway spotlight swinging onto a garment that is unmistakably hers
- Beats: (1) the crowd gasps at her stolen collection; (2) Nadia in the back row, phone raised, recording; (3) the turn: she live-posts the original sketches, timestamped two years earlier; (4) the audience's phones light up, one by one
- Cliffhanger: the partner spots her in the crowd, freeze on his face
- Keyframe scenes: spotlight garment / back-row recording / timestamped sketches on a phone / his frozen face

### 4. Interactive / comment-driven episodes, the audience votes, the story obeys

**The format.** One decision per episode, and the decision is genuinely handed to the viewers: the episode freezes on the choice, the vote runs natively in the comments, and the *next* episode plays out the winning choice. The comment section becomes part of the writers' room. The vote mechanic is now platform-native: TikTok's comment polls, rolled out globally on Sept 3, 2026, give creators up to five options, a creator-set timeframe, and real-time results tracked in the comment thread (TechCrunch / USA Today, Sept 2026). The platform's own suggested uses include voting on the next video idea: the interactive format is the serialized form of that exact behavior.

**Why it's verified, not trend-hype.** This is the strongest new sub-format of the cycle, with evidence on both sides of the fence:

- **Interactive production is now a stated product category.** Singapore-based DRAMAGO (an AI-native drama platform) announced Sept 30, 2026 that it has built its catalogue around interactive drama since April 2026, 14 AI-produced dramas released, 10 of them interactive, and plans a Q4 2026 beta of an "AI Story World" where the audience keeps questioning the story after the episode ends (FinanceWire press release, Sept 30, 2026, company-claimed).
- **The audience is already doing it on TikTok.** Sydney Robinson's (@thatgirlsydjo) five-part "Group Chat" series, fictional drama unfolding between a group of friends, played by one creator, opened at 30M+ views and 20,000 comments of viewers demanding more episodes (Dexerto). A vertical-micro-drama survey paper (Zenodo, late 2025) documents the behavior explicitly: viewers *roleplay in the comments*, anticipating characters' next moves, "effectively becoming a shared communal experience." Some micro-drama apps have already built in-app discussion threads and polls so viewers vote on plot twists (same paper). TikTok has been adapting too: an experimental "Minis" series section in the main app and, by early 2026, PineDrama as a separate app to organize episodic shorts with continue-watching rails.

**Why it works.** Participation is a stronger follow mechanic than emotion. A cliffhanger asks the viewer to *return*; a vote asks them to *invest*, and investment converts: the voter has to come back to see whether their choice won. The comment section does double duty as distribution (comments are engagement signals) and as the writers' room (the winning vote and the strongest minority theories become episode N+1's block inputs).

**The pipeline rules for this format:**

- **One decision per episode**, the interactive analogue of the two-emotions rule. Two votes splits the comment section and kills the funnel.
- **The decision beat freezes on the choice**, generate a freeze-frame-friendly keyframe with clean composition; do NOT burn the poll into the video. The native comment poll does the asking, it stays editable, tallies itself, and enforces the deadline.
- **The vote gets a real deadline** ("the winning choice plays out tomorrow"), open votes feel like homework; closed votes feel like a game. The comment poll's built-in timeframe *is* the deadline: set it when you post, not in a pinned comment after.
- **The vote wins, always**, rigging or ignoring the result reads instantly in the comments. The format's contract is participation.
- **Harvest the comments**, the winning vote and the loudest minority theories become the next block's stakes, hook, and beats. Log the poll tally from the in-thread results into the arc tracker. TikTok's Sept 2026 comment overhaul made the comments a media surface, voice comments (up to 60s, 18+) and photo comments roll out alongside polls (TechCrunch, Sept 2026), so the loudest minority theories may arrive as audio: transcribe before harvesting.

**Worked episode-block example** *(fictional):*

- Format: interactive · Episode 3 · Emotion: **suspense**
- Stake: Lena finds a door in her apartment that was not there yesterday
- Hook visual (first 3s): a door where a wall should be, light leaking underneath
- Beats: (1) the impossible door; (2) the vote: she knocks, or walks away (the decision beat, freeze on her hand); (3) she follows the winning choice, the consequence plays out; (4) the turn: what is behind the door reframes the question
- Cliffhanger: the next decision point, freeze before the vote closes
- Keyframe scenes: impossible-door close-up / decision-beat freeze (native poll UI asks, no burned text) / consequence beat / decision-point cliffhanger

*Honesty note on the rest of the cycle:* multi-POV telling (the Group Chat phenomenon is inherently multi-character) is a *technique inside* these formats, not a verified standalone AI format; duet/stitch chains are a 2020-era mechanic, not new; and "ask the AI character" Q&A accounts (e.g. the Eleanor account's "ask AI anything") show no verified Oct-2026 serialized-mini-drama traction, reported as observed, not as a format pick.

*Revisit #6 (wave 38):* no new verified formats this cycle. The ReelShort economics above are monetization data, not a new format; Vidu S2 is real-time avatar tech (a different product class, see the Stage 5 tooling note); DRAMAGO's interactive slate and the comment-poll mechanics stand from wave 32. Four formats + the honesty note stand.

## Studio 2.0, the pipeline's production-planning end

The guide's [Studio](../studio.html) now runs the episode pipeline as a planning tool end to end:

- **Series mode**, plan 3 to 10 episodes in one pass. Each episode is a full production plan (shot list with per-shot prompts from the 47-template library, per-shot model picks from `models.json` with real cost math, budget lines, schedule), wrapped in a **series bible**: locked cast anchors + locations and a **prompt-DNA block** prepended verbatim to every shot prompt in every episode, the pipeline's official cross-episode consistency engine.
- **The bridge**, "Send series to Studio →" in the [Episode planner](../episode-planner.html) stages the saved series (title, logline, cast anchors, every block's format/runtime/beats) into the Studio, which pre-fills project type (most common block format), episode count (block count, 3 to 10), per-episode runtime (median beats × seconds-per-beat snapped into the format's band), cast rows, and attaches each block's emotion/beats/hook/turn/cliffhanger as the episode's arc, no skeletons when bridge arcs exist. "Send run to Studio →" stages the same saved series into the Studio's **microdrama mode** instead: episode count + median runtime per episode flow into the clip budget, the $50/min benchmark, the retake budget, and the timeline.
- **Microdrama mode**, the Studio's economics planner for serialized microdrama runs (Studio 2.5): episodes + minutes per episode + quality tier in → clip budget in 10 to 15s clip units, per-episode and run budgets against the documented $50/min benchmark priced with live `models.json` rates, the 3 to 5× "drawing cards" retake budget (draft plans the low end, festival the high end), a character-regeneration reserve line, PUGC revenue context, and a timeline from the documented 4-days-for-4-episodes pace. Every number carries its documented basis, ranges, not promises.
- **The production packet**, the deliverable: the full costed packet (bible, per-episode arcs + shot prompts with locked DNA, model picks, budget with the "saved by the bible" reuse line, schedule, the consistency checklist) exported as Markdown or a self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, a print stylesheet, and zero external requests.

**The reference implementation.** A full 5-episode mini-drama, *"The Night Bus"*, runs through this whole chain in `~/workspace/tiktok-episode-pipeline/WORKED-EXAMPLE-5-EPISODE.md`: concept → five planner blocks → the bridge handoff → a Studio series packet with real cost math (50 shots, $20.48 clean / $102.40 at 5× / $409.60 at 20×, seed `b272deb1`), and the nine gates walked for episode 1. The numbers are asserted against the real engine in `scripts/agent-workflows.test.js` (workflow 5), if the underlying model data changes, the test fails rather than letting the example drift.

**A documented build.** TheWrap's StoReel Canvas experiment (June 2026) is the most honestly documented AI microdrama build: four one-minute episodes in four days for ~$150 of credits, a 50-page script from one prompt (Claude, five minutes), a one-click breakdown into characters + settings + a 146-clip storyboard, 300 to 400-word stage-direction prompts per 10 to 15s clip, and paid character regenerations when faces drifted. The pipeline shape matches the nine stages above, and the failures match the skipped stages: the reporter never edited the AI-generated stage directions, so the acting came out wooden and a wall went missing mid-scene. Qidian Interactive's Wuxi studio (Sixth Tone, June 2026) runs the professional version of the same flow: three small groups (characters + settings, generation, edit, one to two people each), a reusable digital prop room, and the industry's "drawing cards" retake discipline (three to five attempts per usable shot). See the full shot-by-shot teardown ([teardown.html](../teardown.html), "The $150 Microdrama"). The Studio's [microdrama mode](../studio.html?mode=microdrama) plans runs from these same figures, clip budget, benchmark, retake envelope, regen reserve, timeline.

All four formats plug into the same planner. The [Episode planner](../episode-planner.html) now has a **format picker** (mini-drama / POV series / day-in-the-life / revenge arc / interactive) that pre-fills the block skeleton per format, plus a **runtime estimator** (beats × seconds-per-beat) that checks the estimate against the genre's runtime band before you save, the dialogue-budget rule, enforced at the planning stage instead of discovered in post.

## The nine stages, adapted

The production pipeline runs one episode at a time inside a series scaffold built once. Per the research artifact:

1. **Series setup (once):** series config (name, hashtag, voices, episode counter), a character bible with one fixed anchor paragraph + one verified reference image + one locked voice *per character*, and the full 3-act arc (8 to 12 episodes) with a per-episode block for every episode. Cast: 2 to 4 characters; no new characters mid-episode. *Craft note: the bible is a contract. Redesigning a face mid-series is not iteration, it is a continuity failure the audience reads as a new character.*
2. **Episode prep:** pull the episode block from the arc, one emotion, hook visual for the first 3 seconds, cliffhanger. Write the caption *first*, from the formula, before shooting anything. If the caption for episode 1 isn't clickable, the series isn't ready.
3. **Script:** 8 to 12 lines of spoken-form dialogue, characters talk *to each other*, no narrator, soap-opera pacing (hook line → banter → gut-punch → cliffhanger question). Spoken-form rules: spell out numbers, no stage directions, no markup. Read it aloud: hook line lands in line 1, last line is a question or an interrupted beat, never a resolution.
4. **Voice first, lock the dialogue track before any image work.** Synthesize the full script for a duration check (8 to 12 lines ≈ 60 to 90s; cutting words is free, re-cutting video is not), then synthesize per line, decode to WAV (never concat MP3s, junk leading frames silently eat segments), concat, and verify the total equals the sum of the parts to the frame. Per-line durations *are* the edit map: line boundaries are guaranteed word-gap-safe cut points. No forced alignment needed. First word starts ≤0.3s from t=0, the genre has no establishing lead-in.

*Tooling note (Oct 2026):* a new top-ranked voice engine entered the field, HeyGen Voice (Oct 9, 2026) debuted at #1 on Artificial Analysis' independent TTS leaderboard (Elo 1,201, blind human tests; company announcement via PR Newswire; reporting via tipranks.com, vibeleaderboard.ai). The API is list-priced at $30/million characters with a $15/million-character launch price through Oct 31, 2026 (vibeleaderboard.ai, verify live), and free in-platform access. The trade-off for episode production is speed, not quality: ~40 characters/second makes it slow for realtime agents but fine for Stage 3's batch per-line synthesis, per-line WAVs don't need low latency. Whatever engine you pick, the pipeline's voice contract doesn't change: same voice ID for every line of a character, locked in the bible, verified by the duration concat. Leaderboard position is launch-week; lock the engine once and never swap mid-series, G9 discipline beats a better Elo.

*Consent is a production gate now.* The Oct 2026 Royal Mail/ElevenLabs episode, an AI-generated voiceover on a Christmas ad, no regulator action but public backlash (research notes), and the 80+ performer petition for a legal right to own one's voice (Save Our Voices Now, founded by actor Peter Caulfield and backed by Nicola Coughlan, via Pinsent Mason) mean the bible's voice line needs a rights column: own the voice, license it, or synthesize it from scratch. Cloning a real person's voice without explicit consent is how a series dies before episode 2. (HeyGen's Professional Voice Clone tier, $99/mo, builds explicit consent into the product.)
5. **Keyframes:** 3 to 4 vertical 9:16 stills per episode, each anchored on the locked character reference image plus the anchor paragraph verbatim, scene description, and an explicit no-text-in-frame instruction. Scene plan per episode: (1) hook shot = caption restated visually, (2) beat coverage, (3) the emotional turn's *dedicated* shot, (4) cliffhanger shot. The turn and the cliffhanger each get their own keyframe, never share a shot with the setup. Verify every keyframe before animating: on-model, text-free, 9:16. *Craft note: faces are a one-time decision. A bible character with a real expressive mouth can lip-sync; a locked flat face (dot eyes, stitched smile) must stay still forever, with voice and burned captions carrying the dialogue. Prompting mouth motion on a locked face doesn't add acting, it redesigns the character (pink noses, eyebrows, anime eyes).*

*Tooling note (Oct 2026):* multi-reference video models accept the bible's locked anchor plates directly, Vidu Q4 Preview (launched Oct 7, 2026) takes up to 15 image references and 3 audio references, with list pricing $0.045/s at 540p to $0.39/s at 4K (PR Newswire, the $0.014/s launch headline was a promotional off-peak floor, not a list rate; preview pricing, verify live). Kling 4.0's announced Omni Reference works the same way, but the full model was still not GA as of Oct 11, 2026 (Flash early access only), use the bible's plates, not a model you don't have.

*Tooling note (wave 38, Oct 2026):* the animation tier moved down-market this cycle. **Wan 3.0** (formal release Aug 24, 2026) does 2 to 30s clips with native audio at a **$0.05/s provider-list rate at 480p** (reported benchmark, verify live), the current cost floor for Stage 5 animation and continuation clips; render long at 480p, upscale after. The draft tier: **Gemini Omni Flash** at ~**$0.03/s at 360p** (~$0.10/s at 720p, token-billed; reported benchmark, verify live), the "draft cheap" half of the Studio's draft-final optimizer mode (wave 34): block the episode at 360p, finish the keeper takes at full res. Mid-tier: **FLUX 3 Video** at $0.06/s 720p draft / $0.17/s 1080p HD (API, verify live). All rates from the guide's `models.json` (last_verified 2026-10-11), verify live before budgeting.

*Editorial rule, brief to the row, not the headline.* versely.studio's Oct 2026 state-of-video generalizes the wave-30 headline-price rule to specs: vendor headline specs ≠ the hosted row's actual specs (Wan 3.0's row renders 15s, not the vendor's 30s; MiniMax H3 Max's row is 768p, not 1080p). The production packet's model table quotes the row you actually rendered on, resolution, duration, rate, with the vendor claim in a footnote, never the reverse. G5 gains a sub-check: every rate in the budget traces to a row, not a headline.

*Hype hygiene for model picks:* **Veo 4 does not exist.** The top-ranking "Veo 4 release date" pages are SEO bait; Google's latest official video model remains **Veo 3.1** (Oct 2025), I/O 2026's move was Gemini Omni, a conversational platform, not a Veo 4 (lumeflow, verified across three sources). Never plan a series around a rumored model.

*Honest mapping for the real-time tier:* **Vidu S2** (Sept 15, 2026, S2-Avatar real-time 720p interactive, S2-Editing on live streams; PR Newswire) is a different product class from rendered clips, it does not enter the Stage 5 budget. Its pipeline relevance is the interactive format's *live companion* lane (the off-screen-lives technique from wave 32): an S2 avatar can host the comment-poll results show between episodes. Cheapest paid tier ~$0.05/clip reported, verify live (`models.json`).
6. **Animation:** animate each keyframe, slow push-ins and small gestures, never fast or busy motion. Verify a mid-clip frame for every clip before building the episode around it. If footage falls short of the dialogue duration: up to 9% short, apply a uniform `setpts` slowdown (K ≤ 1.09, imperceptible on slow push-ins); more than that, generate a continuation clip, new frames, same scene. Never reuse or rewind a clip; never let one clip cover two non-adjacent lines.
7. **Assembly, the reproducible cut.** Cut the picture *to the voice*: line boundaries from the duration table are the cut points, and every cut must sit in silence (check the waveform ±0.1s). Never cut mid-word. Bed audio at −18dB under dialogue. Captions burned in as phrase-level ASS (explicit 1080×1920 script resolution, SRT burned through libass without it renders at 384×288 and balloons to poster size). Final duration must hug the dialogue track within ±10%.

*Procedure fork (wave 38, Oct 2026):* Adobe's **Sept 8, 2026 multi-model workbench** embeds five competing models, Firefly, Google Veo, Runway, Kling, Luma, directly in Premiere's toolbar (TechTimes, ~Sept 9): generative B-roll and continuation clips happen in-timeline with no round-trip export, plus in-timeline AI audio/music generation and audio-repair tools (an After Effects AI assistant shipped alongside). This forks Stage 6 into two documented paths: **(A) build-cut.sh**, the pipeline's reference assembly, ffmpeg piece table, reproducible from scratch (the default); **(B) in-timeline**, generate continuation clips and the bed inside the NLE, cut to the locked dialogue track, keep the piece table as sequence markers. Path B trades reproducibility for speed, so the discipline carries over: name every clip by its line number, cut only in the inter-line gaps, export the XML/EDL with the episode, and every AI-generated clip still gets the mid-frame verification. What the workbench does not change: G3 (the dialogue track locks first, audio repair polishes a locked track, it never re-times it) and the ±10% runtime rule. Same read as the Dragon Blue teardown: cast the model to its bias per shot (Seedance leans pro-EPK, Veo leans run-and-gun, wave 33). **Mirage Tesseract** (launched Sept 22, 2026, EZ Newswire, agent-driven editing and motion-graphics suite, free local engine) slots into Stages 6 to 7 as the motion-graphics hand: animated title cards, lower-thirds, caption treatments. It is an edit/post tool, not a generation model, it never generates episode footage.
8. **Caption package:** the hook-title caption, hook line first (never lead with hashtags), the character named every time (new viewers meet them in the caption), one emoji doing emotional work, the tease as the CTA ("part N+1 tomorrow", finales get the thesis line instead). Posting discipline: watch once on a phone, first frame = hook visual, one episode per day, never dump multiple episodes at once. Turn on TikTok's AIGC label for AI episodes, it does not affect distribution when the video is guidelines-compliant (TikTok Newsroom, Oct 1, 2026); skipping the label is the risk, not the label itself.
9. **Continuity:** append to the episode log (number, title, emotion, hook, cliffhanger, duration, what worked) and add at least one production lesson, story, timing, or production. Increment the episode counter. Bible discipline holds: anchors, ref images, and voice IDs never change mid-series; if a character must evolve, do it between acts, log it as a deliberate revision, and issue a new ref image.

*Verification side-note (wave 38):* Google's **SynthID Detector** launched publicly **Oct 7, 2026** (Google X post; corroborated ×6 sources): it verifies Google watermarks, the verdict reads "made or edited with Google AI," and the video view splits picture vs audio with watermark marks; sign-in via Google/OpenAI/Apple; ~10 checks/day; **terms ban scripts and automated submissions** (manual, one file at a time). Useful for checking the provenance of received stock/UGC footage, it is not a pipeline stage (no batch verification), and SynthID-only detection means a negative result is not proof of authenticity.

## The golden rule

**Picture is cut TO the locked dialogue track, never the reverse.** The dialogue duration is the episode's budget; the total runtime hugs it within ±10%. This ordering is the entire production advantage: voice is cheap to iterate (cutting words is free) and expensive to waste (re-cutting video is not). Every stage after voice exists to serve the track, not to negotiate with it.

## Hard budgets

| Resource | Limit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Video generations per episode | ≤ 6 clips | Platform caps and focus; trim hard, best 2 to 4s slice wins |
| Keyframe generations per episode | ≤ 4 stills | Forces the 4-shot scene plan; fewer, better coverage |
| Dialogue start | ≤ 0.3s from t=0 | Genre rule, the hook line IS the opening shot |
| Runtime vs dialogue | ±10% | Edit feels tight; beyond it the cut reads sloppy |
| Uniform picture slowdown | K ≤ 1.09 | Invisible on slow push-ins; beyond that looks smeary |
| Footage usage | ~50 to 60% of generated | Trim ruthlessly; coverage is not the episode |
| Bed audio | −18dB under dialogue | Dialogue always intelligible; the bed is felt, not heard |
| Captions | Phrase-level, never overlapping | Start = first word − 0.05s, end = last word + 0.25s |

These budgets are genre-plastic in one direction only: you can spend *fewer* videos or *less* runtime. Spending more on any row is how episodes die in post.

## The nine quality gates

Run every episode through all nine before it ships. A gate fails → fix at that stage, never compensate downstream.

- [ ] **G0, Series lock:** bible has anchor + verified ref image + locked voice per character; arc complete with all episode blocks and cliffhangers.
- [ ] **G2, Script:** read aloud; hook line in line 1; one emotion; ends mid-beat (question or interrupted line, never a resolution).
- [ ] **G3, Voice:** `dialogue.wav` duration equals the sum of line durations; total in the 60 to 150s band; no line exceeds ~12s.
- [ ] **G4, Keyframes:** on-model, text-free, 9:16; dedicated shots for the emotional turn and the cliffhanger.
- [ ] **G5, Clips:** every clip's mid-frame verified on-model; total usable footage within −9%/+40% of dialogue; clip count ≤ 6.
- [ ] **G6, Cut:** 1080×1920; runtime ±10% of dialogue; dialogue starts ≤0.3s; captions burned, phrase-level, legible; the assembly script re-runs cleanly from scratch.
- [ ] **G7, Caption package:** hook + hashtags + tease; one-episode-per-day cadence respected.
- [ ] **G8, Continuity:** episode log + lesson appended; episode counter incremented.
- [ ] **G9, Cross-episode consistency (series gate):** prompt-DNA block byte-identical across every shot prompt of every episode; anchor paragraphs byte-identical to the bible; no new characters mid-episode; recurring props/costumes carried across episodes per the bible. (Run once per season, or whenever the bible changes.)

(Gates are numbered to match the pipeline stages, G1, the per-episode prep check, is absorbed into the episode block itself.)

## Worked example: one episode end to end, the interactive format (wave 38)

Everything above, walked once, with real numbers. The series: **"The Seventh Floor"**, an interactive mini-drama. Lena, a night-shift nurse, finds a door in her apartment hallway that was not there yesterday. The episode ends on the decision, knock or walk away, and the TikTok comment poll decides. Every number below is asserted against the guide's `data/v1/models.json` (last_verified 2026-10-11); verify live before spending.

**Concept → episode block** (as saved in the [Episode planner](../episode-planner.html), interactive preset):

- Format: interactive · Episode 1 · Emotion: **suspense**
- Stake: Lena finds a door in her apartment that was not there yesterday
- Hook visual (first 3s): a door where a wall should be, light leaking underneath
- Beats: (1) Hook: Lena stares at the impossible door; (2) she counts the hallway doors, six yesterday, seven today; (3) the turn: the light under the door goes out, like something inside noticed her; (4) the decision beat: her hand hovers, knock or walk away (freeze on her hand; the native comment poll asks, up to 5 options, never burned into the video)
- Cliffhanger: the poll is live, the winning choice plays out tomorrow
- Keyframe scenes: impossible-door close-up / hallway count / light-dies turn / hand-hover decision freeze

**Bible entries (G0):** Lena, anchor: "a 29-year-old woman with short black hair, tired kind eyes, wearing faded teal hospital scrubs"; voice: `avocado_v2:MAI_03` (locked); Mrs. Okafor, anchor: "a 60-year-old woman with silver-streaked braided hair, gold-rimmed glasses, wearing a patterned housecoat"; voice: `avocado_v2:MAI_01` (locked). One prompt-DNA block, prepended verbatim to every generation prompt in every episode: *"9:16 vertical, muted hallway-night palette, soft practical lighting, no text, no words, no letters, no watermarks anywhere in frame."*

**TTS script** (Stage 2, spoken form; numbers spelled out, no stage directions):

```
Lena: There are six doors in this hallway. I have counted them every night for three years.
Lena: One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six. And… seven.
Lena: Seven doors. Light is coming from under the seventh.
Neighbor: Lena? It is two in the morning. Are you all right out there?
Lena: Mrs. Okafor, tell me how many doors are in this hallway.
Mrs. Okafor: Six, dear. The same six as always. Now go to bed.
Lena: Then why can I see light coming from under the seventh one?
Mrs. Okafor: There is no seventh door, Lena. There has never been a seventh door.
Lena: It just went dark. The light under it went out, like something inside noticed me standing here.
Mrs. Okafor: Whatever you do, do not knock. I am begging you. Do not knock on that door.
Lena: My hand is on the wood. Cold air is coming through the keyhole. It is breathing.
Lena: Knock… or walk away? You decide. The poll is open until tomorrow.
```

12 lines, 155 words, 790 spoken characters → ≈60 to 75s of dialogue at natural TTS pace with inter-line gaps: inside the interactive format's 60 to 150s band. The read-aloud test: hook line lands in line 1, one emotion (suspense) throughout, the last line is the decision, not a resolution. Stage 3 is authoritative, the synthesized `dialogue.wav` duration is the episode's budget, and the final cut must hug it within ±10%.

**Keyframe prompts** (Stage 4, anchor paragraph verbatim + DNA block + scene + no-text instruction):

```
[image: references/refs/lena.png]
a 29-year-old woman with short black hair, tired kind eyes, wearing faded teal
hospital scrubs. She stands frozen in a dim apartment hallway, staring at a
wooden door that should not exist, warm light leaking from beneath it.
9:16 vertical, muted hallway-night palette, soft practical lighting,
no text, no words, no letters, no watermarks anywhere in frame.
```

The four shots: (1) the impossible-door close-up (the hook = the caption restated visually), (2) Lena counting doors down the hallway, (3) the turn, the light under the door gone, her face half-lit, (4) the decision freeze, her hand hovering inches from the wood, clean composition for the poll. The turn and the decision each get their own keyframe, never shared with the setup.

**Animation prompts** (Stage 5, slow, small): `"slow push-in toward the glowing door seam, Lena's hand rising into frame"`; `"slow drift down the hallway past six doors, settling on the seventh"`; `"static frame, the light under the door dying out"`; `"slow push-in on the hovering hand, trembling slightly"`. Mid-clip frames verified on-model for all four before the cut is built.

**Budget, real model data, both paths:**

| Line | Rate (from `models.json`) | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Voice, 790 chars, HeyGen Voice API | $30/M chars list ($15/M launch through Oct 31) | **$0.024** ($0.012 at launch) |
| 4 keyframes, Higgsfield Soul 2.0 | 0.12 credits/image; Plus $47/1200cr = $0.0392/cr | **$0.019** |
| Animation Path A, 4 clips × 5s, Vidu Q4 I2V 1080p | $0.12/s list, 30% off I2V through Nov 30 → **$0.084/s** (the row rate, not the $0.014/s headline) | **$1.68** |
| Animation Path B (budget), 4 clips × 5s, Wan 3.0 480p | $0.05/s provider-list | **$1.00** |
| Optional draft pass, Gemini Omni Flash 360p | $0.03/s | $0.60 |
| **Episode total, Path A, clean** | | **$1.72** |
| **Episode total, Path A, at 5× drawing-cards** | | **$8.61** |

Against the Studio's $50/min microdrama benchmark: 62s ≈ 1.03 minutes → benchmark $51.67. The 5× envelope ($8.61) is 17% of benchmark, the bible's reuse math doing its work on episode 1 already, before any cross-episode savings. (Draft pass is the Studio 3.0 "draft cheap, finish flagship" mode: $0.60 of 360p drafts before the keeper takes.)

**Caption package** (Stage 7, from the [Hook-title generator](../hook-generator.html), vote variant):

```
Episode 1, Lena found a door in her apartment that was not there yesterday 🚪
#theseventhfloor #aianimation #fyp #emotionalstory
vote in the comments, the winning choice plays out tomorrow 🗳️
```

**Quality-gate walk:** G0, bible locked (2 anchors + verified refs + 2 locked voices), arc has all 8 episode blocks with cliffhangers; G2, read aloud, hook in line 1, one emotion, ends on the decision; G3, `dialogue.wav` == Σ line WAVs, ≈62s in the 60 to 150s band; G4, 4 keyframes on-model, text-free, 9:16, dedicated turn + decision shots; G5, mid-clip frames verified, footage within −9%/+40%, 4 clips ≤ 6; G6, 1080×1920, runtime ±10% of dialogue, dialogue ≤0.3s in, phrase-level burned captions; G7, caption = hook + hashtags + vote tease, posted once; G8, log + lesson appended, counter incremented; G9, prompt-DNA byte-identical across all shot prompts, anchors byte-identical to the bible, no new characters mid-episode.

*The night after posting:* harvest the poll tally from the in-thread results into the arc tracker, the winning vote and the loudest minority theories become episode 2's stakes, hook, and beats. The vote wins, always.

## Worked example: one episode end to end, the revenge-arc volume format (revisit #7)

The interactive example above is the craft-format episode. This one is the money-format episode, the revenge arc that pays for the industry. The economics changed this cycle, so the example carries them: ByteDance launched **Dramagic** (Sept 21, 2026), a full-pipeline AI short-drama platform from script analysis to video previews, sold through BytePlus (the-decoder.com, secondary trade press); the China Netcasting Services Association counts ~128,000 short dramas published in China in Q1 2026, three times all of the previous year, with ~95% AI-generated (via the-decoder); Tsinghua's Shen Yang puts a minute of AI video at **$90 to 120**, about a tenth of traditional (via the-decoder); Caixin's cover reporting has contract prices collapsing from 800 to 1,000 yuan/minute to **200 yuan/minute**, with a 100-minute AI drama now producible in 3 to 7 days for under 20,000 yuan (reported, paywalled, treat the figures as reported); Quartz/Sensor Tower put US microdrama in-app revenue at **$3B in 2025, +115% YoY**, $11B globally (multi-outlet verified). On the prestige end, Inkitt's Ironblood makes AI microdramas in 3 to 4 weeks for ≤$60,000, human-written, actors brought in to train the models on expressions, a human director prompting revisions in minutes (bworldonline, Aug 2026). The format below is the solo-creator version of that pipeline: human script, AI execution, the nine gates intact.

The series: **"The Wrong Heir"**, a revenge-arc mini-drama. Jia, 28, is about to be toasted at her own engagement party when she opens the ring box and finds a stranger's ring. The episode ends before she speaks. Every number below is asserted against the guide's `data/v1/pricing.json` (Seedance 2.0 tiers) and `models.json`; verify live before spending.

**Concept → episode block** (as saved in the [Episode planner](../episode-planner.html), revenge-arc preset):

- Format: revenge-arc · Episode 1 · Emotion: **cold fury**
- Stake: at her engagement party, Jia opens the ring box and finds a fake, and spots the real ring on her future mother-in-law's hand
- Hook visual (first 3s): the box clicks open on a stone she has never seen
- Beats: (1) Hook: the box opens, wrong ring; (2) the proof: her grandmother's ring had a chipped band, this one is flawless; (3) the turn: across the room, Mrs. Chen raises her champagne, wearing the chipped band; (4) the freeze: Jia smiles at the room, raises her glass, and pockets the fake (clean composition for the episode-2 tease)
- Cliffhanger: the toast is in ten minutes, what does she say?
- Keyframe scenes: box-open close-up / the flawless band macro / Mrs. Chen's hand across the room / Jia's smile with the pocketed box

**Bible entries (G0):** Jia, anchor: "a 28-year-old woman with a sharp black bob, jade stud earrings, wearing a crimson qipao"; voice: `avocado_v2:MAI_03` (locked); Mrs. Chen, anchor: "a 60-year-old woman with a silver-streaked chignon, heavy gold bangles, wearing an emerald silk jacket"; voice: `avocado_v2:MAI_01` (locked). One prompt-DNA block, prepended verbatim to every generation prompt in every episode: *"9:16 vertical, warm banquet-hall palette, candlelit practicals, no text, no words, no letters, no watermarks anywhere in frame."*

**TTS script** (Stage 2, spoken form):

```
Jia: Ten minutes until the toast. My hands are shaking so badly I can barely open the box.
Jia: This is not my ring.
Jia: My grandmother's ring had a chip on the band. She dropped it the winter I was born. This band is flawless.
Jia: Someone switched the rings. At my own engagement party.
Mrs. Chen: Jia, darling. Come, everyone is waiting for the toast.
Jia: Coming, Mrs. Chen. That is a beautiful ring you are wearing tonight.
Mrs. Chen: Oh, this old thing. A family piece.
Jia: The chipped band. I would know it anywhere.
Jia: She is wearing my grandmother's ring. And smiling at me.
Jia: Ten minutes until the toast. I am going to smile back.
Jia: Episode two, the toast. You do not want to miss it.
```

11 lines, 148 words, 745 spoken characters → ≈60 to 70s of dialogue: inside the revenge-arc band. One emotion (cold fury) throughout; the last line is the tease, never the resolution. Stage 3 is authoritative, the synthesized `dialogue.wav` duration is the episode's budget, and the final cut hugs it within ±10%.

**Keyframe prompts** (Stage 4, anchor verbatim + DNA + no-text): the box-open macro (the hook = the caption restated visually); the flawless band in extreme close-up; Mrs. Chen's bangled hand across the candlelit room, the chipped band catching light (the turn gets its own keyframe, never borrowed); Jia's composed smile, one hand sliding the box into her pocket.

**Animation prompts** (Stage 5, slow, small): `"slow push-in on the opening box, the wrong stone catching candlelight"`; `"macro drift along the flawless band"`; `"slow rack from Mrs. Chen's smile to her hand, the chipped band glinting"`; `"slow push-in on Jia's smile as her hand pockets the box"`. Mid-clip frames verified on-model before the cut.

**Budget, real pricing-table data, both paths:**

| Line | Rate (from `pricing.json`) | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Voice, 745 chars, HeyGen Voice API | $30/M chars list ($15/M launch through Oct 31) | **$0.022** ($0.011 at launch) |
| 4 keyframes, Higgsfield Soul 2.0 | 0.12 credits/image; Plus $47/1200cr = $0.0392/cr | **$0.019** |
| Animation Path A, 4 clips × 5s, Seedance 2.0 720p | $0.08/s third-party estimate, verify live | **$1.60** |
| Animation Path B (budget), 4 clips × 5s, Wan 3.0 480p | $0.05/s provider-list | **$1.00** |
| **Episode total, Path A, clean** | | **$1.64** |
| **Episode total, Path A, at 5× drawing-cards** | | **$8.20** |

Against the Studio's $50/min benchmark: 65s ≈ 1.08 minutes → benchmark $54.17. The 5× envelope ($8.20) is 15% of benchmark, the same bible-reuse math as the interactive example, in the format the market actually pays for. (A vendor piece claims $500 to 1,000 for a full 10-episode AI series vs $15,000 to 50,000 traditional, single-source, vendor-published; the per-episode math above is the checkable version of that claim.)

**Caption package** (Stage 7, from the [Hook-title generator](../hook-generator.html)):

```
Episode 1, She opened the ring box at her own engagement party… and it was the wrong ring 💍
#thewrongheir #aianimation #fyp #revengearc
episode 2, the toast. tomorrow.
```

**Quality-gate walk:** G0, bible locked (2 anchors + verified refs + 2 locked voices); G2, read aloud, hook in line 1, one emotion (cold fury), ends on the tease; G3, `dialogue.wav` in the 60 to 150s band; G4, 4 keyframes on-model, text-free, 9:16, dedicated turn shot; G5, mid-clip frames verified; G6, 1080×1920, runtime ±10% of dialogue; G7, caption = hook + hashtags + tease; G8, log + lesson; G9, prompt-DNA byte-identical, anchors byte-identical.

*Revisit #7 honesty line:* no new verified episode *formats* this cycle, the revenge arc stands from the planner presets. What's new is the volume economics (Dramagic, the Q1 2026 output figures, the 200-yuan/minute contract floor) and the second worked example proving the pipeline's per-episode math holds in the commercial format, not just the craft one.

## Craft judgment: where pipelines break

- **The turn without a shot.** If your script has an emotional turn but your scene plan has no keyframe for it, you will "borrow" a beat shot in the edit and the turn will land flat. Dedicated turn shot, or rewrite the turn into a line that plays on a face you already have.
- **Two emotions, one episode.** The read-aloud test catches it: if the script makes you feel grief *and* relief, it is two episodes stapled together. Split it.
- **Dialogue drift.** The line-boundary table is only trustworthy if the voice IDs never change and the concat is verified to the frame. One skipped verification and every cut downstream is a guess.
- **The bible is a social contract with your audience.** Every mid-series redesign resets the viewer's memory of who your character is, in a genre where the cast is the brand, that is the costliest failure available.
- **The oversupply discipline.** DataEye's H1 2026 numbers, 221,900 new AI dramas on Douyin, a 0.48% hit rate, 98.7% never breaking even, are not a reason to post more episodes. They are the reason each episode goes through all nine gates. In a market where footage is nearly free, the only scarce inputs are the ones this chapter makes expensive: the locked bible, the read-aloud script, the verified voice track, the dedicated turn shot. Spend your discipline where the market can't cheapen it.
- **The one-prompt temptation.** Text-to-full-story tools now exist inside the platforms themselves: TikTok's Symphony Agent generates complete ad campaigns from a prompt (on Seedance 2.0), and CapCut's Video Studio advertises type-an-idea → multi-scene emotional mini-dramas (Metricool 2026 timeline; a creator post, treat as directional). They are useful for *drafting beats*, but they skip the locked bible, the voice-first cut, and the continuity log, exactly the three things that turn a pile of episodes into a series. Draft with them if you like; ship from the pipeline.
