<!-- chapter: legal/script-clearance.md -->
# Script Clearance: The Report, the Chain, and the Gate

**Not legal advice.** What follows is the script-clearance system as documented in the clearance literature researched for this guide (research cycle 81, Identity r78, Film script-clearance rules 1358 to 1367, from six sources fetched in full: an entertainment law firm's clearance guidelines, WIPO's rights-clearance guide for independent filmmakers, an entertainment lawyer's account, a law-office clearance FAQ, an insurer's E&O page, and a film-insurance coverage note). It describes what the documents are, when each is required, and how a production assembles them. It invents no legal claims beyond those sources; where the research is silent, this chapter says so. Clearance for a real production belongs with a clearance researcher and an entertainment attorney.

The guide's rights chapter covers disclosure, likeness, and music. This chapter covers the layer underneath all of them: **what may lawfully appear in the work at all**, every name, place, business, object, and the title itself, researched against the real world before and during production, and proved in a file that an insurer and a distributor will both demand to see.

## The system in one pass

1. The **final shooting script** is researched by a professional clearance researcher; the result is the **clearance report** (rule 1358).
2. The writer supplies an **annotation guide** labelling every character, place, and event fictional, real, or composite (rule 1359).
3. Names, businesses, and addresses that coincide with real, identifiable people or entities are changed or released; only **permitted telephone and plate numbers** ever appear (rule 1360).
4. Ownership is proved as an unbroken **chain of title**, verified by a **copyright report** (rule 1361).
5. The film's own title is researched in a **title report** before final selection (rule 1362).
6. Written **releases** cover depicted persons, performers, extras, crew, and distinctive locations (rule 1363).
7. Featured **props, products, artwork, and photographs** are cleared one by one, under an abundance of caution (rule 1364).
8. The report is a **living document**, updated whenever new material enters, at every stage (rule 1365).
9. Every flagged item closes with a **recorded decision**, license, substitute, change the use, or expressly assume the risk (rule 1366).
10. Before exhibition, the **finished film is checked against the file**, trailers get their own analysis, and the completed file is the **gate**: no completed clearance, no E&O cover and no distribution (rule 1367).

The working tool built on these ten rules, a clearance file you can run an AI-film production through, item by item, with the gate verdict computed from your own entries, is the guide's [Script clearance desk](../clearance.html).

## The clearance report (rule 1358)

**What it is.** The system's founding document, commissioned rather than improvised: a professional clearance research company researches the final shooting script. Every story character name and place is checked against how common that name, street address, and business name actually is in the general population, so a fictional person does not accidentally coincide with a real one who could claim to have been portrayed. The same report identifies the proper contact from whom to obtain permission for any product, copyright, or trademark the script references. WIPO's guide states the same instrument from the producer's side: the clearance report, prepared by a legal expert, is the key document structuring the whole process, it identifies the objects and materials in the project that carry infringement risk, and it can carry title reports and clearance/release submission logs as attached parts.

**When it is required.** Before production, the report is filed on the final shooting script, and (rule 1365) it does not stop there.

**How a production assembles it.** Lock the shooting script; send it, with the annotation guide below, to the clearance researcher; file the returned report as the production's master clearance record, with the title report and release logs attached.

## The annotation guide (rule 1359)

**What it is.** A document the writer supplies, identifying every character, place, and event in the script and stating whether each is purely fictional, real, or a composite of real and fictitious material, because that label is what determines which further releases are needed. Two companion records pin the work's origins down: the stimulus and sequence by which an "original" unpublished work was created are documented, and if a similar script by a different writer was ever submitted to the same company, the wholly independent path of the later script is documented and evaluated, so an infringement claim can be answered from the file. For true-life stories the discipline extends to sources: whether the writer relied on independent, primary sources (contemporaneous reports, court transcripts, public records) or on secondary, copyrighted works, the latter ordinarily requiring a release. A law-office FAQ states the same starting point in plain form: the review begins from an annotated script describing every character, place, and event, real or fictitious, and everything based on underlying property.

**When it is required.** At the start, it is the clearance review's input, not its output.

**How a production assembles it.** The writer annotates the script element by element (fictional / real / composite), documents the work's origins and any similar submission's independent path, and records true-life sources as primary or secondary.

## Researched names and permitted numbers (rule 1360)

**What it is.** The day-to-day substance of the research is names. Every single character's name in the script is checked, against the possibility that a real person with that exact name believes they are being portrayed without permission; all proposed signage for stores, institutions, and other locations is researched against copyright and trademark restrictions; and only certain phone and license plate numbers may be used at all, the permitted-number discipline that keeps a fictional number from ringing a real subscriber. The insurer's page states the failure mode the research prevents as a named coverage class: claims arising from character names, business names, addresses, or other identifying details in the screenplay that match real-world individuals or entities, which is why a full script clearance search precedes production.

**The rule.** A fictional name, business, or address that coincides with a real, identifiable person or entity is changed or released before use, coincidence is a defect, not a defence, and only permitted telephone and plate numbers ever appear.

**For AI-film productions.** Generated signage, storefronts, documents, and plates are exactly where unresearched names and numbers slip in, a model will happily render a plausible business name that belongs to someone. The research is silent on AI-generated signage as a special case; the rule above is stated for scripts, and this guide applies it to anything the finished film shows, because rule 1367's final check covers what the script never contained. That application is the guide's practice, labelled as such, not a claim from the research.

## Chain of title and the copyright report (rule 1361)

**What it is.** Under the script sits the property record. The producer documents the origin of the work and each transaction that transferred rights in it up to the producer, the chain of title, testing whether the writer's engagement was a bona fide work for hire and, if not, whether an effective option or transfer exists; potential rights-holders are identified (including contributors under earlier, expired options whose rewrite contributions may outlive them), anyone who contributed content without giving a release is found, and quitclaims are obtained from anyone holding an encumbrance on a clean chain. A separate copyright report verifies the chain, domestic and foreign copyrights and renewal rights, and is always required by distributors; a party acquiring a completed film performs the same review again on the underlying property. WIPO states the stakes in one line of structure: the chain of title is the unbroken record of ownership, and it is a condition for the film's circulation in the market, expressly asserted to distributors and sales agents.

**When it is required.** From acquisition onward, and again at delivery, when the distributor and the acquirer re-run the review.

**How a production assembles it.** File the origin document and every transfer in order; test each work-for-hire or option; find unreleased contributors; quitclaim encumbrances; commission the copyright report covering domestic, foreign, and renewal rights. The guide's rights chapter makes the same point from the AI side: an AI track or image produces a thin rights file, and the paperwork is where that thinness is caught.

## The title report (rule 1362)

**What it is.** The film's own name goes through the same discipline as its characters'. A title report is obtained prior to final title selection: it sets out prior uses of the same or similar titles, and if there is a conflict, the title is changed; for an additional fee the reporting company adds a legal opinion on whether the title is clear. Distributors require the report, and the E&O application file shows why: the application itself includes a title report completed by a title search company, expressly to ensure the production's title is not too similar to an existing production. At the end of the process the title is chosen and again submitted for research, against the real frequency of same-and-similar titles already released.

**The rule.** A work's title is researched before final selection; the report lists prior same and similar uses, a conflict changes the title, and the report is filed for the distributors and insurers who require it.

## Release coverage (rule 1363)

**What it is.** What the report flags is closed with paper. Written releases from living persons recognizably depicted, a class that expressly includes thinly disguised versions and persons identifiable through other characters or the factual, historical, or geographic setting, and, for deceased persons, from their personal representatives or heirs; insurers insist on these unless the production demonstrates in writing why a release is unnecessary. Performers and recognizable extras release not just image and name but the production's rights to edit, delete, juxtapose, and fictionalize; crew contracts carry likeness releases too, against the day a crew member is captured on camera or in behind-the-scenes footage. Distinctive locations, buildings, businesses, and personal property filmed get written releases; non-distinctive background use usually does not. A law-office FAQ's three-category form, property, people, locations, matches the same coverage, with releases from all persons appearing, crew included.

**The rule.** Written releases cover every recognizably depicted person, thinly disguised and deceased included, the latter via representatives or heirs, every performer, recognizable extra and crew member, and every distinctive location.

## The featured-object caution (rule 1364)

**What it is.** Props, set dressing, and wardrobe bearing distinctive logos are cleared, under a stated abundance of caution, because a prop's prominence in the final cut cannot be anticipated, and items from prop houses or prior films are never assumed already cleared. Artwork demands the same caution in full, even unfocused work, with the artist, their death date, first publication, and copyright holder all established; photographs and posters need releases from photographer, subject, and holder alike.

**The rule.** Props, products, artwork, and photographs are cleared one by one under an abundance of caution, prominence in the final form is unknowable in advance, and supplied or previously used items are never assumed already cleared.

**For AI-film productions.** A generated frame is full of featured objects nobody placed there deliberately: artwork on a wall, a poster, a product on a shelf. The research addresses props and artwork in shot productions; it is silent on generated set dressing as a category. The guide's practice, clear what the finished film prominently shows, item by item, at the final check, follows from rules 1364 and 1367 read together, and is labelled as practice, not as a researched claim.

## The living report (rule 1365)

**What it is.** Clearance does not end at the script. The report can and should be updated as more materials are included, in the script, the schedule, the storyboard, the actual shooting, and even postproduction, extending to shot-by-shot analysis. Clearance starts as early as possible, with preproduction as the latest responsible start, because late-found rights are the expensive kind. Filmmaker and attorney monitor the production at all stages, from inception through final cut.

**The rule.** The clearance report is updated whenever new material enters, script versions, boards, schedules, the shoot, post-production, and clearance monitoring runs at all stages, not as a single pass at the start.

## The recorded decision (rule 1366)

**What it is.** Each flagged item is closed by a decision, taken with the legal expert: license the content, substitute a different element, use it in a different way, or keep the use as it is without licensing, an express assumption of risk, recorded as such.

**The rule.** Every flagged item is closed by a recorded decision, license it, substitute it, change the way it is used, or expressly assume the risk, and an undecided flagged item blocks the element it flags. The clearance desk's gate verdict is this rule, computed: one open flag holds the gate.

## The final check and the E&O / distribution gate (rule 1367)

**What it is.** Before any public exhibition the attorney previews the finished film to assure the procedures were followed, because the film contains things no script ever listed: the lawyer's account describes the rough version reviewed precisely for what slipped in, a protected mark caught in the background of an outdoor shot. Advertising is not inherited clearance: trailers and commercial tie-ins get a separate analysis that licenses extend to publicity use, and bonus content is cleared like the primary production. Known rights problems arising after application must still be disclosed to the insurer. The completed file is what the gates check: without completed clearance procedures there is no E&O policy, and without an E&O policy the distributors and platforms will not license or acquire the film at all. E&O itself is content-liability cover, defamation, copyright infringement, invasion of privacy, required by distributors and platforms before licensing or acquisition, and script-clearance failures are one of its named claim classes.

**The E&O application file**, as the coverage note itemises it: the producer's biography, the script, synopsis, and production copy for review, the clearance reports, and a title report completed by a title search company. The insurer's 12-point clearance checklist likewise opens with chain of title and full-cast script clearance, and carries ongoing disclosure and bonus-content clearance as standing items.

**The rule.** Before exhibition the finished work is reviewed against the clearance file for what the script never contained, trailers and publicity receive their own clearance analysis, and the completed file is the gate, no completed clearance, no cover and no distribution.

## What the research does not say

Honesty about the edges, in the guide's usual form:

- The six sources describe the system for conventionally produced films. Their application to AI-generated material in this chapter is marked, each time, as the guide's practice derived from the rules, the sources do not address generative pipelines, model outputs, or synthetic performers.
- The sources name no prices, turnaround times, or named clearance companies' rates for any document above, and this chapter quotes none.
- The sources are US-practice documents (plus WIPO's international guide). Jurisdiction-specific requirements beyond what is stated here are outside the research; the chapter does not generalise them.
- Nothing here is legal advice, and no checklist in this guide substitutes for a clearance researcher and an entertainment attorney on a real production.

<!-- chapter: platforms/field-guide.md -->
# AI Video Platform Field Guide

Every major platform, honestly assessed. Strengths, weaknesses, costs, and what each is actually best at.

## The field

| Platform | Signature strength | Weakness | Cost signal | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Higgsfield** | All-in-one: many engines, Soul ID, Cinema Studio presets, camera moves | Preset UI hides raw controls; shared credit pool obscures per-model price | Basic 120 / Pro 600 / Max 1,800 credits/mo; tiers Free to Premium (10+ credits) | Filmmaking workflow, character-led series |
| **Kling** (direct) | Photoreal physics (water, fire, smoke); end-frame pinning; multi-reference `elements` | Prompt engineering required, no hand-holding | ~0.6 units/sec 720p standard (~$0.084/sec); 0.8 pro; 3.0 native 4K | Hero shots when you want raw control |
| **Runway** (Gen-3/Gen-4) | Reference-image start + Motion Brush for exact motion control; human-centric scenes | Weaker without a strong start image | Paid tiers, full commercial rights | Ads, human scenes, precise motion |
| **Sora** (discontinued Mar 2026) | n/a |, | n/a | Migrate to Kling 3.0 or Veo 3.1 |
| **Luma Dream Machine** | Cinematic experimentation, smooth motion | Consistency weaker than leaders | Varies | Dreamlike / experimental passages |
| **Pika** | Lip-sync, character animation, playful effects; most permissive creatively | Less "cinematic" out of the box | Subscription | Dialogue, social, stylized work |
| **Hailuo / MiniMax** | VFX and fluid motion | Prompt nuance | Mid tier | Action, fluid dynamics |
| **Veo** | Nature/landscapes, reference-image fidelity, long coherent passages | Premium cost | Premium tier | Landscapes, documentary feel |
| **Wan** | Artistic / stylized video | Less photoreal | Mid tier | Stylized sequences |
| **Seedance** | Fast iteration speed | Top-end polish trails Kling | Mid tier | Drafting, volume work |

## Platform-specific prompting notes

- **Sora (discontinued Mar 2026):** historical note only, prompts-as-mini-screenplays worked for vast scenes; migrate that thinking to Kling 3.0 or Veo 3.1.
- **Runway:** start with a strong reference image, then Motion Brush for movement. More predictable than text-only.
- **Kling:** keep prompts concise and direct; elaborate prose underperforms. Use motion templates.
- **Pika:** stack creative effects; for lip-sync feed clean audio with minimal background noise.

## Ownership and rights (verify before commercial use)

- Runway: full commercial rights on paid tiers.
- Kling: commercial rights on Pro and above.
- Pika: full ownership on paid tiers; free tier restricts commercial use.

## The honest take

No single platform wins every shot. Festival-grade films are hybrid: pick the engine per shot, match color in post, and nobody will know. See `when-to-use-what.md`.

- https://github.com/servanter/ai-magic/blob/HEAD/content/blog/best-ai-video-generators-2026-sora-runway-kling-pika-comparison.mdx
- https://www.meltflexai.com/blog/higgsfield-alternatives
- https://dyerbolical.com/mastering-ai-video-generation-in-2026-runway-pika-and-kling-for-professional-ads/

<!-- chapter: platforms/when-to-use-what.md -->
# When to Use What

The decision tree for picking the right tool per shot. Festival-grade films are hybrid, nobody will know if you match color in post.

## Decision rules

| Shot need | Reach for | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Character close-up / dialogue | Higgsfield + Soul ID (Kling 3.0 engine) | Identity lock + top-tier faces + native audio |
| Epic scale / impossible environments | Kling 3.0 | Native 4K, best vast-scene physics (Sora discontinued Mar 2026, see Model watch) |
| Nature / landscapes | Veo 3.1 | Reference-image fidelity, natural texture |
| Precise motion control | Runway + Motion Brush | Paint exactly where movement happens |
| Fast action / fluid VFX | Hailuo 2.3 | Fluid dynamics strength |
| Stylized / artistic passages | Wan 2.6 | Style over photorealism |
| Lip-sync dialogue | Pika | Clean-audio-in, synced lips out |
| Drafting / volume / tests | Seedance 2.0 Pro or Kling 2.5 Turbo | Speed and cost |
| Budget hero on a budget | Kling direct (end-frame pinning, elements) | Raw control without preset markup |

## The hybrid pipeline

1. **Plan per shot, not per film.** The shot list gets a model assignment column.
2. **Anchor on one identity system** (Soul ID) so faces survive platform-hopping.
3. **Generate in passes:** all drafts on cheap/fast models → approve → heroes on premium.
4. **Normalize in post:** one color pipeline, one grain overlay, one audio mix. This is what makes mixed sources invisible.
5. **Never switch models mid-scene** unless you have to, consistency is cheaper than correction.

## Cost-aware ordering

- Rough out the whole film on Turbo/Lite first (cheap).
- Identify the 10 to 15 hero shots that carry the story.
- Spend premium credits only on heroes and dialogue.
- Everything else ships from the draft pass with a good grade.

## Anti-patterns

- Using one platform for everything out of loyalty, you pay in quality somewhere.
- Premium-rendering a shot before the edit is locked, re-edits waste the expensive generation.
- Mixing aspect ratios across shots, pick delivery format on day one.

<!-- chapter: economics/credit-math.md -->
# Credit Math

Professional quality without burning the budget. The standing rule: **never spend credits on a guess.**

## What things cost (Higgsfield)

| Plan | Credits/mo | Rough video yield |
|---|---|---|
| Basic | 120 | ~15 standard clips |
| Pro | 600 | ~75 standard clips |
| Max | 1,800 | ~225 standard clips |

Model tiers: Free (Soul 2.0, DoP Lite) · Low (0.1 to 2 credits) · Mid (2 to 10) · Premium (10+). A standard Kling clip runs ~8 credits; premium/longer/Cinema Studio sessions cost more.

Going direct to Kling: ~$0.084/sec at 720p standard, ~$0.112/sec pro, ~$0.42/sec native 4K. Credits **reset each billing cycle and don't roll over**, schedule production so paid credits don't evaporate.

## The no-guess pipeline (credit-saving order of operations)

1. **Write the shot list first.** Every clip planned before a single credit is spent.
2. **Draft cheap.** Turbo/Lite models for composition and motion tests.
3. **Render heroes expensive.** Premium models only for faces, dialogue, and key story beats.
4. **One clip at a time, quality-gated.** A failed clip never chains, re-prompt, don't hope.
5. **Price before you send.** Estimate cost per request before batching; verify balance before a batch, not after.

## Where to spend vs save

- **Spend:** hero close-ups, dialogue shots, the trailer moment, the final shot.
- **Save:** establishers, B-roll, transitions, montages, Turbo is fine.
- **Free tools that don't look free:** CapCut for color/LUTs/grain, stabilization in post instead of re-rendering, compositing fixes (face swaps from close shots) instead of regenerating wide shots.

## The short-film budget frame

A 3 to 5 minute festival film at ~4 seconds per shot is 45 to 75 shots. At draft-then-hero discipline, most shots need 2 to 4 generations to land. Budget for 150 to 300 generations and plan the credit pool before starting, or split across platforms by shot type.

## Per-clip costs across platforms (third-party estimates, Oct 2026, re-verify before budgeting)

| Platform | Est. cost per clip | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Vidu | ~$0.05 | Cheapest; free tier non-commercial |
| PixVerse | ~$0.07 | Budget pick |
| Pika | ~$0.17 to 0.61 | Standard plan has NO commercial use, trap |
| Hailuo (MiniMax) | ~$0.44 to 0.76 | Best price/quality ratio per multiple sources |
| Luma | ~$0.30 to 1.20 | |
| Kling 3.0 | ~$0.40 | Strong motion/camera control |
| Veo 3.1 Fast | ~$0.40 to 0.50 | Native audio; cheapest premium-quality route |
| Runway Gen-4.5 | ~$1.44 to 1.50 | Fastest generation |
| Higgsfield (Seedance 2.5) | ~$2.48 | Aggregates many models |
| Sora 2 | discontinued Mar 2026 | Do not plan new work on it |

## Rules of thumb from working filmmakers

- **~$80 per finished minute** of film, all-in.
- **3 to 5 takes per keeper; 2 to 5x raw-to-finished multiplier.** Budget the rejects, not the hero renders.
- **$40 to 165 in credits** for a disciplined 3-minute short; $150 to 300+ without discipline.
- **Resolution ladder:** 480p drafts → 720/1080p heroes → upscale to 4K in post (native 4K ≈ $1/sec).
- **Audio-first:** lock voiceover/soundtrack before generating video, cheap audio prevents expensive timing-mismatch re-rolls.
- **Cautionary:** one documented Higgsfield pilot burned ~$260,000 in credits over 4 days for ~8 usable shots, brute-force iteration without craft. The no-guess rule exists because of math like this.

## Try it

Run your numbers in the [interactive budget calculator](../budget.html), runtime, shot length, model, and discipline in, cost envelope out.

## Sources
- https://www.thehypemagazine.com/2026/10/09/what-is-higgsfield-ai-uses-features-pricing/
- https://www.meltflexai.com/blog/higgsfield-alternatives
- http://dev.to/mckennachapman/higgsfield-api-in-practice-prompt-to-editorial-photo-and-the-defaults-that-bite-f0c
- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z8IaWHEYfpY

<!-- chapter: case-studies/competition-teardowns.md -->
# Competition teardowns

Shot-by-shot craft lessons from films that placed in judged AI-film competitions. Every entry below was found with an attributed source, nothing invented. Items the research could not verify are flagged.

## The pattern before the films

Across Runway AIFF, Project Odyssey, Reply AIFF, the Higgsfield Action Contest, and MIT's hackathon, judges reward the same things: **story over spectacle, authorial intent, character/POV discipline, originality, sound design, and polish as the floor.** They punish: visible morphing/inconsistency, generic "AI slop," tech demos without narrative, and AI that pulls focus from the story.

Distilled: narrative cohesion + committed POV + intentional AI use + pro-grade sound + consistent visuals. Originality is the tiebreaker; polish is the entry ticket.

## The case studies

### "Total Pixel Space", Jacob Adler, Runway AIFF 2025 Grand Prix
9:28 essay film. A voiceover calculates how many possible images could exist in digital space; surreal tableaux illustrate it. Inspired by Borges' "The Library of Babel." Tools: image generators + synthetic voices + Runway Gen-3; over a year in production, tens of thousands of images. Field: ~6,000 submissions; judges included Harmony Korine and Gaspar Noé.
**Why it won:** concept-first, AI-thematic, the medium is the message. The critic's take: it treats AI's glitches and eeriness as material to think with, carried by old-fashioned style and narrative. **Steal:** make the film *about* what the medium does, or make the medium invisible, never halfway.

### "Get Me Out", Daniel Antebi, Runway AIFF 2024 Grand Prix
6 min. Aka flees a shadowy suburban house that stores his haunting memories, embodied by a blood-red figure of pure muscle. About displacement and mental health. Tools: Luma (3D environment capture), Runway video-to-video, ComfyUI (rotoscoped a performer, re-skinned him as muscle).
**Why it won:** hybrid craft, live-action emotional performance with invisible, motivated AI VFX. Antebi's own read: the artist-jurors resonated with the storytelling, not the tool cleverness. **Steal:** shoot the emotion for real; use AI only for what the budget couldn't do otherwise.

### "A Face Only a Mother Could Love", Robert Gaudette, Runway AIFF 2026 Grand Prix + Reply AIFF 2026 winner
Photorealistic short: Marcel, a solitary Parisian dancer born with facial disfigurement; a woman's approach sparks connection. Tools: Grok, Nano Banana, Seedance, chosen, in his words, as the only viable way to film the screenplay without budget, cast, or crew. It started as an old screenplay experiment, never meant for festivals.
**Why it won:** intimacy and POV, tight shots establishing point of view in a way reviewers don't associate with AI imagery; nothing read as slop. **Steal:** a real screenplay beats a prompt. Character-first photorealism is now a proven winning lane.

### "GRANDMA vs WASP", Muhannad Nassar & Simon Meyer, Higgsfield Action Contest winner
Action short. The duo never met in person, async remote workflow across time zones in Higgsfield's Cinema Studio. Field: 8,752 submissions, 139 countries. Judges (Jason Zada, Buralqy, Jama Jurabaev) prioritized storytelling and directorial intent over technical polish.
**Why it won:** proof that decentralized AI production works, two strangers, one film, no studio. **Steal:** team up across disciplines; judges reward directorial intent, not solo prompt heroics.

### "CUPID", Nikolay Shestak, Higgsfield Action Contest finalist
Tagline: "Aggression has become the norm. It's time for silence." Shestak is an established actor/filmmaker using Higgsfield for concepts that would need prohibitive traditional budgets.
**Why it won:** the archetype judges love, a professional using AI for impossible scale, not novelty. **Steal:** bring a filmmaker's eye; the tool is the budget, not the idea.

### "SCRATCH", Ash & Aram Gevorkyan, Higgsfield Action Contest finalist
High-production-value action short/trailer, made in **five days** by a director/musician + 3D/VFX generalist duo. Early Higgsfield adopters with commercial music-video fluency. Audiences mistook it for a studio-backed theatrical trailer.
**Why it won:** deep tool fluency plus trailer-form craft, sound, cutting, pacing. **Steal:** five days of fluent execution beats five weeks of hesitant prompting. Learn the tool until it's invisible.

### "One Last Wish", Project Odyssey S2 Narrative Gold
An elderly inmate's final wish. Made in **48 hours** at a Norwegian AI-film workshop: a real screenwriter's script, a director, a dedicated AI-visuals artist, and a dedicated editor/sound designer.
**Why it won:** professional division of labor. A real script plus dedicated edit and sound beat solo prompting in the narrative category. **Steal:** split the roles even on a tiny team, never let the prompter also be the sound designer.

### "Le Drip", Alex Naghavi & Ezra Li, Reply AIFF 2026 2nd
Animated short: a fish's final day on Earth, rendered as living oil paintings, dense textured brushstrokes moving across the screen.
**Why it placed:** a committed, authored art style instead of chasing photorealism. **Steal:** a strong style is a consistency strategy, painterly motion hides the seams photorealism exposes.

### "Jailbird", Andrew Salter, Runway AIFF 2025 2nd
A chicken's journey, from the bird's POV, to a UK prison to join a rehabilitation program. Absurdist comedy in a 6,000-entry field.
**Why it placed:** high-concept premise plus total POV discipline. **Steal:** bold premise + locked POV stands out more than another beautiful drifting landscape.

### "Generation", Riccardo Fusetti, Runway AIFF 2023 Grand Prix (inaugural)
Contemporary dance/performance fused with massive VFX and philosophical voiceover (Gen-1-era restyle).
**Why it won:** expressive, bold mixed-media authorship carried it in the festival's first year. **Steal:** performance plus stylization is a durable formula, the human body gives AI imagery something to hold onto.

### Also noted
"Centenarian Kindergarten" (2xLabs, Reply 2026 3rd + AI-for-Good), "The Child of the Sea" (Ibai Abad, Reply special mention, tactile stop-motion universe on an impossible budget), "For Pixi" (NYU team, MIT Hackathon Best Character), "DO NOT DISTURB THE SANE MAN" (Odyssey S2 Open Format Gold), and AAIFF 2026 winners from 8,067 entries across 125 countries.

## The cautionary case

A much-hyped contest winner was panned for three-eyed cyclopses, size-shifting characters, and feet-for-hands. Press called it a showcase of AI filmmaking's current limits. **Lesson: no hype forgives broken continuity. Consistency is the floor, not the ceiling.**

## What to steal, the winner's checklist

- [ ] A real story with a turn, not a vibe reel
- [ ] AI invisible, or the film is *about* AI imagery, never halfway
- [ ] Committed POV held across every shot
- [ ] Sound designed like a film, not a slideshow (custom music, real voice actors, layered foley)
- [ ] Zero visible morphing, consistency is the entry ticket
- [ ] Human craft felt on screen: a script, an edit, a mix, not just prompts

<!-- chapter: case-studies/entry-craft-teardowns.md -->
# Entry Craft Teardowns: How the Winning Films Were Actually Made

The companion chapter lists *what placed and why*. This one is the *how*, the production techniques behind judged entries, broken into steps you can copy. Every teardown follows the same shape: **the technique**, **the craft principle**, **copy it** (actionable steps), and the **budget/time footprint** where it's documented.

## 1. The async remote workflow, "GRANDMA vs WASP" ($150K, Higgsfield Action Contest)

**The technique.** Directors Muhannad Nassar and Simon Meyer never met in person. They built the film async across time zones inside Higgsfield's Cinema Studio, one shared project where generations, prompts, and assets were all visible to both collaborators. No studio, no set, no shoot days; the "set" was a shared generation window.

**The craft principle.** Judges (Jason Zada, Buralqy, Jama Jurabaev) said they prioritized storytelling and directorial intent over technical polish, in a field of 8,752 submissions from 139 countries. The remote workflow won because the *directing* was centralized even though the *labor* was distributed: one vision, two executors, zero drift between them.

**Copy it.**
- Write a one-page director's intent doc before generating anything: logline, tone references, the single emotion each act must land.
- Work in a shared project, not DMs, every prompt, generation, and select lives where your collaborator can see and fork it.
- Split by discipline, not by scene: one person owns performance/character, the other owns camera/action. Review each other's selects daily.
- Lock a style bible on day one (one style line, aspect ratio, grain/grade, lens language) so two people can't drift apart.

**Footprint.** Two people, zero travel, consumer AI subscriptions. The budget went to time, not gear.

## 2. The five-day sprint, "SCRATCH" ($50K, Higgsfield Action Contest)

**The technique.** Director/musician Ash Gevorkyan + 3D/VFX generalist Aram Gevorkyan made a trailer-grade action short in five days. Audiences mistook it for a studio-backed theatrical trailer. The weapon was trailer form: sound, cutting, and pacing doing the heavy lifting while the imagery stayed in short, high-energy bursts that never linger long enough to break.

**The craft principle.** Fluency beats time. Five days of fluent execution beats five weeks of hesitant prompting, because the duo already knew their tools cold, every generation was a deliberate choice, not an experiment.

**Copy it.**
- Cut a trailer, not a short: 60 to 90 seconds, three acts (hook / escalation / title card), music-driven pacing.
- Keep shots short (2 to 4 seconds). Short shots hide consistency breaks; long takes expose them.
- Build the sound design first or in parallel, trailer percussion, risers, and hard-hitting SFX sell "studio" more than any pixel does.
- Budget generations per shot: 3 to 5 variations for hero shots, 1 to 2 for connective tissue. Decide selects fast.

**Footprint.** Five days, two specialists, deep tool fluency. The most replicable winning formula in this chapter.

## 3. The hybrid pipeline, "Passport Rush" and "Get Me Out"

**The technique.** "Passport Rush" combined hand-drawn storyboards + Blender previz + AI animation, publishing every prompt and asset. "Get Me Out" (Runway AIFF 2024 Grand Prix) captured a real 3D environment in Luma, shot a real performer, then used Runway video-to-video and ComfyUI to rotoscope and re-skin him as a blood-red muscle figure.

**The craft principle.** Shoot the emotion for real; use AI only for what the budget couldn't do otherwise. Both films put a human performance or human draftsmanship at the center and used AI as the *impossible* layer, never the *entire* layer. Jurors (working artists, in Antebi's case) resonated with the storytelling, not the tool cleverness.

**Copy it.**
- Board on paper or in Blender first. If the story doesn't work as boards, it won't work as generations.
- Capture or shoot anything with a human body in it for real, even a phone previz gives the AI motion something truthful to hold onto.
- Use video-to-video / motion transfer for transformation, not text-to-video for invention. Transforming real motion beats inventing motion.
- Keep one "truth anchor" per scene (a real plate, a real performance, a real drawing) and let AI handle the other 80%.

**Footprint.** "Get Me Out" was a solo-plus-tools production; "Passport Rush" published its full pipeline as a teaching resource. Both prove hybrid beats pure-generation for emotional weight.

## 4. The authored-style strategy, "Le Drip," "The Tale of the Peony," "The Child of the Sea"

**The technique.** "Le Drip" (Reply AIFF 2026 2nd) rendered a fish's final day as living oil paintings, dense textured brushstrokes in motion. "The Tale of the Peony" (MEGA 2026 Best AI Short) used AI keyframe animation + rice-paper texture + manual keyframe refinement. "The Child of the Sea" built a tactile stop-motion universe.

**The craft principle.** A strong, committed art style is a *consistency strategy*. Painterly motion, rice-paper grain, and stop-motion stepping all hide the seams that photorealism exposes. Judges reward authored intent: pick a lane and commit so hard the style becomes the film's identity.

**Copy it.**
- Choose your style for what it *forgives*, not just what it looks like. Ask: "what breaks when this style drifts 5%?" If the answer is "nothing visible," it's a good judged-category style.
- Lock the style in one sentence and put it verbatim in every prompt ([STYLE] block discipline).
- Add the texture in a separate pass: film grain, paper texture, brushstroke overlays in post unify generations from different models.
- For stylized work, use the animated prompt register, no lens or DOF language (see `prompt-engineering.md`).

**Footprint.** Style commitment costs nothing in credits and buys the most consistency per dollar of any technique here.

## 5. The photoreal character piece, "A Face Only a Mother Could Love" (Runway AIFF 2026 Grand Prix + Reply AIFF 2026)

**The technique.** Robert Gaudette started with an old screenplay, a real script about Marcel, a solitary Parisian dancer, and chose Grok, Nano Banana, and Seedance as, in his words, the only viable way to film it without budget, cast, or crew. Tight shots established point of view in a way reviewers don't associate with AI imagery.

**The craft principle.** A real screenplay beats a prompt. Character-first photorealism with locked POV is now a proven winning lane: intimacy and perspective discipline make AI imagery read as *cinema* instead of *demo*.

**Copy it.**
- Write (or adapt) a real script first, dialogue, beats, turns. If it works on the page, the AI only has to execute.
- Hold one POV ruthlessly. Every shot should answer "whose eyes are we in?" before "what does it look like?"
- Favor tight shots over wides for character pieces: close-ups carry performance; wides expose geometry the models can't hold.
- Cast the models to the job: photoreal portrait models for faces, motion-strong models for body movement, don't ask one model to do both.

**Footprint.** One filmmaker, a screenplay, three models. Proof that writing is the cheapest VFX.

## 6. The long-form discipline, "Oneiric" (20 min) and "Total Pixel Space" (9:28, Runway AIFF 2025 Grand Prix)

**The technique.** "Oneiric" ran a 20-minute drama through Cinema Studio with open-sourced everything: every Seedance asset and prompt, Claude skills for scripting/acting/prompting, a color-coded Diagram Skill frame map tracking every shot, and a consistent-lens-look trick for visual unity. (Correction: earlier versions of this guide repeated a "Cannes premiere" claim for Oneiric, dedicated research found no source for it. It was made for Higgsfield's own film festival; the Cannes-adjacent screening was *Hell Grind's*, a third-party industry showcase, not an official selection.) "Total Pixel Space" spent over a year in production generating tens of thousands of images for a 9-minute essay film.

**The craft principle.** Long-form AI filmmaking is *asset management*, not prompting. The winners built production systems, frame maps, skill libraries, lens-look rules, that let hundreds of generations cohere. Time in pre-production and systems pays back exponentially at 10+ minutes.

**Copy it.**
- Build a frame map before generating: every shot on a timeline with its lens, lighting, and character state, color-coded by status.
- Separate identity from motion in every prompt (Identity Block vs Motion Block), at feature length, this is the difference between a cast and a crowd of strangers.
- Validate at 720p, upscale only winners. At long-form scale, rendering everything at max quality first is how budgets die.
- Re-anchor references every few generations, don't wait for drift to become visible.
- Use J/L cuts and a shared ambience bed to mask transitions; sound covers a multitude of visual sins.

**Footprint.** "Oneiric" was a small team with systems; "Total Pixel Space" was a year of iteration. Both show that long-form is a marathon budgeted in *organization*, not just credits. (Full long-form pipelines get their own chapter in `craft/longform-pipelines.md`.)

## 7. The floor, what kills entries

The cautionary case: a hyped contest winner had three-eyed cyclopses, size-shifting characters, and feet-for-hands. Press called it a showcase of AI filmmaking's current limits. **No hype forgives broken continuity.** Across every festival in the companion chapter, judges punish the same things: visible morphing, generic AI slop, tech demos without narrative, and AI that pulls focus from the story.

**Copy it (in reverse).** Before submitting, run the entry-killer audit:
- [ ] No morphing faces, extra limbs, or shifting wardrobe across cuts
- [ ] No shot exists just to show off a model, every shot serves the story
- [ ] Sound designed like a film (custom music, voice, layered foley), not a slideshow
- [ ] One committed POV or style held across the entire runtime
- [ ] A human edit: pacing, turns, and a button image, not a prompt sequence

## Build your entry like a winner, assembly order

1. **Script first.** A real story with a turn. (Teardowns 5, 6)
2. **Pick your consistency strategy.** Authored style, hybrid truth-anchor, or photoreal POV discipline, choose for what it forgives. (Teardowns 3, 4, 5)
3. **Lock the style bible.** One style line, verbatim, in every prompt. (Teardowns 1, 4)
4. **Board or previz.** Paper, Blender, or phone footage, prove the story before spending credits. (Teardown 3)
5. **Generate in the right order.** Keyframes → motion → selects; 720p drafts, upscale winners only. (Teardown 6)
6. **Cut like a trailer editor.** Short shots, music-driven pacing, J/L cuts. (Teardown 2)
7. **Sound is half the film.** Custom music, real or AI voices with rights, layered foley, ambience bed. (Teardowns 2, 6)
8. **Run the entry-killer audit.** Zero morphing, zero demo shots, committed POV throughout. (Teardown 7)

## 7th teardown research (wave 27, 2026-10-11)
- https://www.thewrap.com/industry-news/tech/off-campus-ai-microdrama-see-the-results-storeel/, StoReel Canvas "Off Campus" experiment: 4 one-minute AI episodes, 4 days, ~$150 (11,000+ credits, 300 free); Claude 50-page script in 5 min; one-click breakdown into characters + settings + 146 clips of 10 to 15s; 300 to 400-word stage-direction prompts per clip (~10 min render per 10s clip); paid character regenerations; wooden acting / vanishing-wall / Steinbeck-to-Steinberg failures; $50/min AI vs $2,000/min live-action; PUGC ~$150/min payouts, 80/20 PUGC split, 100 shows/month goal, 80+ AI originals, Day-7 retention +22% vs live action, CPI $4.63 vs $8 to 10
- https://www.thewrap.com/media-platforms/tv/ai-generated-microdramas-could-be-the-future-of-mobile-entertainment/, AI microdrama industry survey: showrunners feed a page of dialogue ≈ one minute/one episode; engines compatible with Seedance 2.0; scripting 10 days to 1 month + 1 month production for in-house content
- https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018935, Qidian Interactive / Yudian studio (Wuxi): premise-from-trends → dialogue → storyboards → 3D spatial arrangement → cliffhanger assessment; 10+ criteria assessment model; three-group flow (characters+settings / generation / edit, 1 to 2 each) with team-leader review; digital prop room; 3D positioning plug-in; naturalness prompts ("simulate natural daylight" etc.); "drawing cards" discipline (3 to 5 attempts per usable shot, card operators); 4 to 5 dramas/day × 30 to 44 episodes; 1M-yuan AI rebuild of shelved 8 to 10M-yuan 3-year project in 2 months

<!-- chapter: guides/first-short.md -->
# Your First 60-Second Short: A 7-Day Plan

One finished minute. That's the goal, not a masterpiece, a *finished* film. Sixty seconds forces every discipline in this guide into one small, shippable object: story, prompting, generation, selects, sound, grade, export. Follow the days in order. Each day links the exact chapters, skills, and tools to use, and ends with a checkpoint: don't move on until it passes.

**Rules for the week:** one character, one location, no dialogue longer than two short lines (write around talking, visual storytelling wins at this length). Budget: one cheap draft model for days 2 to 3, your best model only for final hero shots. Track spend in the budget calculator as you go.

## Day 1, Concept lock

**Do:** write one logline (protagonist + want + obstacle, one sentence), then a 6-beat outline: setup, turn 1, turn 2, midpoint image, turn 3, button. Pick your one location and describe it in three sensory sentences, this description becomes your style anchor for the whole week.

**Use:** `craft/story-structure.md` (beats), the prompt workshop's logline template (`workshop.html`).

**Checkpoint:** you can pitch the film in 20 seconds without notes. If you can't, the concept isn't locked, simplify until you can.

## Day 2, Prompt workshop session

**Do:** generate your hero frame first, the single perfect still of your character in your location. Lock identity before anything moves (this is the take-casting decision). Then write one full prompt per shot (8 to 12 shots for 60 seconds) using the nine-layer anatomy: subject, action with tactics, setting, light, camera, lens behavior, texture, negative constraints, audio note.

**Use:** `higgsfield/prompt-engineering.md`, `workshop.html` (save your prompts, you'll iterate on them), the `audio-lip-sync-route` skill if you have any dialogue at all.

**Checkpoint:** every prompt has an exclusion block ("no morphing faces, no extra fingers, no text"). No exclusions, no generation.

## Day 3, Generation batches

**Do:** generate in cheap drafts first. Batch each shot 3 to 5 takes on your draft model, then pick selects, don't direct yet, just collect. Price the day before you start (credit math × takes) and hold a credit floor: if spend passes plan by ~15%, stop and re-plan.

**Use:** `platforms/when-to-use-what.md` (or the quiz: `quiz.html`), `economics/credit-math.md`, `budget.html`.

**Checkpoint:** you have selects for every shot, imperfect, but every story beat exists on screen. Gaps get re-prompted tomorrow, not tonight.

## Day 4, Selects & assembly

**Do:** cut the radio edit, selects in story order, no polish. This is where the film either works or doesn't, and it's cheaper to discover now. If a character drifts between shots, fix it with the consistency tools (reference frames, re-generated hero angles) rather than accepting it. Once a take is approved, lock it: re-render the camera around the performance, never the performance around the camera.

**Use:** `craft/editing-pipeline.md`, `craft/character-consistency.md`, `craft/directing-performance.md` (the Scene Lock rule).

**Checkpoint:** the cut plays start to finish and the story reads with the sound off. If it doesn't read silent, no amount of sound will save it.

## Day 5, Performance fixes

**Do:** watch like a director, not a generator. For each shot that feels dead: first try restraint (strip adjectives, give the eyes a job, widen the frame), then try one targeted re-generation, then, if it still fails, cut around it. Read the failure gallery before you re-roll anything: most "bad generations" are direction problems with known fixes.

**Use:** `craft/directing-performance.md`, `craft/failure-gallery.md`, the shot teardown viewer (`teardown.html`) for reference.

**Checkpoint:** no shot embarrasses you. "Good enough" is a finishable standard; "perfect" is how films die at 80%.

## Day 6, Sound

**Do:** build the full audio pass in order: ambient bed under every scene, foley on movement, voice/dialogue on its own track (Road A or B, chosen per scene, never mixed mid-scene), score built cue-by-cue to the locked cut, then the mix (dialogue on top, headroom left, phone-speaker test). Save generation receipts for every AI voice and music cue.

**Use:** `craft/sound-music-audio.md`, the `audio-sfx-bed`, `audio-direct-voiceover`, and `audio-final-mix` skills, the audio checklist at the end of the chapter.

**Checkpoint:** mute the music, the film still plays. Unmute, nothing fights the dialogue.

## Day 7, Grade, mix QC, export

**Do:** apply one consistent grade across all shots (a single LUT or node tree, adjusted per shot, never a different look per shot). Run the mix QC: three listening environments, loudness sane, no clipping. Export to your delivery spec, watch the export all the way through on a different screen than you edited on, then ship it, upload, submit, or screen it for one human.

**Use:** `craft/color-grading.md`, `distribution/release-paths.md` (delivery specs), `legal/rights-and-disclosure.md` (before anything public, disclosure and rights, not legal advice).

**Checkpoint:** a stranger can watch it end-to-end without you explaining anything. That's a finished film. Everything after this is your second one.

## After the week

Do a 20-minute post-mortem while it's fresh: what broke, what the fix was, what you'd prompt differently. Write it down, that's the seed of your personal playbook, and it's worth more than any tutorial. Then start film two: the same 7 days, twice as fast.
